h1: Sourcing oak casks for a craft distillery in India
title: Oak Casks for an Indian Craft Distillery | Craft Beer School
desc: How a craft distillery in India sources oak casks: ex-bourbon, sherry and new oak, checking quality, importing, storage and planning your cask budget.
teaser: Your casks will shape most of your whisky's flavour. Buying them is a supply chain job with a five year horizon.
standfirst: Most of a whisky's flavour comes from the cask, yet new distillers often leave cask sourcing until the stills are installed. In India there is little local cooperage, so planning ahead matters more here than almost anywhere.
sections: Decide what you need before you call anyone

Start with the whisky you want to sell in five or eight years and work back. A light, fruity malt calls for mostly ex-bourbon barrels. A rich, dark style needs sherry or wine casks. A fast-maturing house style in Indian heat might suit refill casks rather than first fill, to avoid over-oaking.

Then put numbers on it: how many litres of new make a year, fill strength, cask size and the share of each cask type. Our guide to whisky inventory planning shows how to work out cask counts from production. Write it down as a cask specification. Suppliers take a written spec far more seriously than a phone call.
The main cask types and where they come from

• Ex-bourbon barrels: American white oak, around 200 litres, from US distilleries. Usually the most available and the best value per litre.
  • Sherry casks: mostly European oak seasoned with sherry in Spain. Far more expensive and often on long lead times.
  • Wine and fortified wine casks: port, red wine and others, used mostly for finishing.
  • New oak: new charred or toasted casks from a cooperage, giving strong flavour fast.
  • Reconditioned casks: shaved, toasted and re-charred, a middle path on cost and flavour.

Some Indian distillers also use Indian or other local oak. Treat any wood new to you as an experiment and trial it before filling at scale. Our guide to whisky maturation and casks covers how each type behaves.

Most small distilleries buy through cask brokers or cooperages that collect, inspect and ship casks. Some deal directly with a source distillery or bodega. Brokers cost more per cask but handle grading, repairs and shipping documents, which is worth a lot for a first order.

Ask each supplier for the cask's history: what it held, for how long, how many fills, the char or toast level and when it was emptied. Ask how they test for leaks and what happens if casks arrive damaged. Get references from other distilleries in hot climates if you can.

Casks are usually shipped whole or broken down into staves and heads, known as shooks, then rebuilt on arrival. Shooks are cheaper to ship but need a cooper at your end. Cooperage skills are scarce in India. Whole casks are simpler but take far more container space.

Imported wood may need plant quarantine clearance and customs documents. Requirements change, so work with an experienced clearing agent and check the current rules before you order. Build in time for delays. A container stuck at port for weeks means dry casks.

Inspect every cask on arrival. Look for cracked staves, loose hoops, mould and off smells. Wine and sherry casks are sometimes treated with sulphur to keep them clean, which can give a struck-match note if not managed.

Casks dry out in transit and in Indian pre-monsoon heat. Swell them with clean water before filling and check for leaks over a day or two. Store empty casks in shade, off the ground and use them soon. Plan arrivals to land just before you need them, not months early.
Budget for the casks, not just the stills

Casks are a big recurring cost and premium cask types can cost several times as much as ex-bourbon. Budget for transport, duty, repairs, rejects and losses as well as the cask itself. Re-using casks for second and third fills spreads the cost, but plan for falling flavour contribution each time.

Track every cask by number: source, type, fill date, strength, warehouse position and regauge results. That record becomes the basis for every blend and every stock valuation you make.
Fill strength and cask choice work together

The strength you fill at changes what the cask gives. Many distillers fill at around 63 to 64% ABV, because some wood compounds extract better at lower strength and others at higher. Filling stronger saves cask space but can change the balance. Decide fill strength with your cask plan, not separately. Keep it consistent so your casks stay comparable.

For a first year, many distillers spread fills across a few cask types and sources rather than betting everything on one supplier. Taste each cask type every few months. By year three you will know which casks suit your spirit and your climate. Then you can order with confidence.
faqs: Where do Indian distilleries get whisky casks?
Mostly imported: ex-bourbon barrels from the US, sherry casks from Spain and wine casks from various regions, usually through brokers or cooperages.
Should I buy whole casks or shooks?
Whole casks are simpler to handle. Shooks save shipping space but need a skilled cooper to rebuild them, which is scarce in India.
How do I stop casks drying out?
Store them in shade, plan deliveries close to filling dates and swell them with clean water before filling. Check for leaks before you fill.
